title: The snow globe was meant to be a lamp
hook: A Viennese snow globe grew out of an attempt to make a brighter lamp.
peek: Around 1900 an instrument maker in Vienna, Erwin Perzy, was trying to make electric light brighter with a glass ball of water. The flakes he floated in it looked like falling snow. His family still makes snow globes in the same city.
lede: Around 1900 Erwin Perzy, a Viennese maker of surgical instruments, was asked for a brighter light. Early electric bulbs were dim, and he tried putting a water-filled glass globe in front of one, a trick cobblers had long used with candles. To scatter more light he added tiny white flakes, including semolina. They did not help the lamp, but they drifted down like snow.

bullets.text: Perzy did not invent the idea outright. Water-filled domes with falling flakes were already shown at the Paris exhibition of 1878. Perzy's version has a separate origin, and he received an early Austrian patent for a snow globe.
Perzy's first globes held a tiny model of the basilica at Mariazell, a pilgrimage town in Austria, sold as a souvenir. Souvenir scenes remain the snow globe's classic use.
Semolina was soon replaced. The family's modern flakes are a closely guarded mixture that sinks slowly and does not yellow in the water, and its recipe has never been made public.
The workshop Perzy founded in Vienna is still run by his family, now with his grandson Erwin Perzy III. It still makes its globes by hand.
